# Preface

It's an awkward time for human exceptionalism: I hear AI's popping bubbles and that math belongs to the machines, now.

Unsatisfied with only catastrophic displacement of the species, it also seems to be keen on telling us that we _might_ just be late to language: Maybe [whales have it too](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspb/article/293/2069/20252994/481340/The-phonology-of-sperm-whale-coda-vowels).

## Roadmap

Science is barreling towards the question of animal linguistics, but the space remains incipient: the tools are new, awareness is sparse, and the knowledge still scattered.

This draft aims to bring you up to speed on the phonology and deep learning needed to make sense of the seminal papers.

I'm not an academic, nor in any way an expert on animal communications. But I know a thing or two about language and ML/DL...So let's just see how far we can get.

---

**Arc I** establishes foundations. It's intended to be self-contained; by the end, you'll have met all the math, linguistics, and deep learning required to review the literature. 

- **Sound & Voice**: [Human language doesn't require speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sign_language), but we start with sound: impulse, rhythm, pitch, and beat. **Planned**.
- **[Sampling & the DFT](04-sampling-dft.ipynb)**: We derive the [Discrete Fourier Transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_Fourier_transform); implement the [STFT](05-stft-spectrograms.ipynb); explore spectral analysis, a foundational technique; and introduce [Mel spectrograms](https://docs.pytorch.org/audio/main/generated/torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram.html), which we use heavily later.
- **Hillenbrand**: We use the classic [Hillenbrand vowel data](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7759650/) to refine our knowledge of vowels, explore [formant normalization](https://marissabarlaz.github.io/portfolio/vowelnormalization/), and review foundational ML/DL.
  - **[Part I](06-hillenbrand-1.ipynb)**: We review EDA, data preprocessing, and explore prior art on the relationship between formants and vowel identification.
  - **[Part II](06-hillenbrand-2-logreg.ipynb)**: We use `sklearn` to fit a baseline `LogisticRegression` model to the tabular formant frequency data, serving as a baseline against later work.
  - **Part III**: We transition to PyTorch, initially using it to replicate Part II's model as a Fully Connected Layer/Softmax architecture. After implementing a series of custom `nn.Module` implementations, we implement MLPs; CNNs; and a ResNet34 architecture, training each on the Mel spectrograms of the Hillenbrand vowel data.

There's a vast gap between ResNet34, by now more than a decade old, and frontier deep learning. But this gives us everything necessary to learn the rest just-in-time.

---

**Arc II** sweeps the literature:

- **Coda Classification with CNNs & RNNs**: We study [Bermant et al.'s result from 2019](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-48909-4), in which they used a CNN to detect sperm whale echolocation clicks, and an RNN to classify coda types. We'll reproduce their results with our own PyTorch implementations.
- **Combinatorial Complexity of Sperm Whale Communications**: Deep learning on codas has exploded since 2019: Coda complexity is known to be radically more complex than then-assumed. We review the most recent knowledge on the matter by reading: 
  - Beguš et al. on [the phonology of sperm whale coda vowels](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspb/article/293/2069/20252994/481340/The-phonology-of-sperm-whale-coda-vowels); [vowel- and diphthong-like spectral patterns in sperm whale codas](https://direct.mit.edu/opmi/article/doi/10.1162/OPMI.a.252/133906/Vowel-and-Diphthong-Like-Spectral-Patterns-in)
  - Sharma et al.'s results on the [unexpected combinatorial complexity of sperm whale coda types](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-47221-8)
  - Gubnitsky et al. on [Automatic detection and annotation of eastern Caribbean sperm whale codas](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40229467/); Gero et al. on [Evidence for the influence of shipping underwater radiated noise on sperm whale coda structure](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8mj8t9h7); and a discussion on the challenges of hydroacoustics, environmental concerns, and the social dynamics of sperm whale clans.  
- **Spectrogram-derived Graph Representations for Audio Deep Learning**: Aironi et al. introduce a [dynamic programming algorithm for creating graph representations of spectrograms](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/356882670_Graph-based_Representation_of_Audio_signals_for_Sound_Event_Classification). We implement and use it to explore characterizations of different coda types.
- **Interlude: Graph Neural Networks**: A paperless interlude introducing [graph neural networks](https://distill.pub/2021/gnn-intro/). We use [PyTorch Geometric](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) to build simple GNNs end-to-end, and dip into [geometric deep learning](https://geometricdeeplearning.com) to understand the relationship between CNNs, GNNs, and Transformers.
- **BirdNET/Xeno-canto Performance Beat with GNNs**: We review the work of Noumida & Rajan, which applied Aironi's methods to [augment BirdNET and produce a claimed SOTA-result on the Xeno-canto dataset](https://pubs.aip.org/asa/jasa/article-abstract/159/4/3598/3387731/Spectrogram-derived-graphs-and-inductive-learning?redirectedFrom=fulltext).
- **Graph-augmented Coda Classification**: We revisit Bermant's 2019 architecture, augmenting it with spectrogram-derived graphs. This is a novel approach and tooling is sparse, so we'll take a quick detour into software engineering to extend [PyTorch Geometric](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) with new utilities for working with audio. We test the architecture rigorously on its original dataset, and then on synthetic codas generated by the [Whale Acoustic Model (WhAM)](https://github.com/Project-CETI/wham/).

--- 

**Arc III** will introduce [mechinterp](https://arena-chapter1-transformer-interp.streamlit.app) in the context of Beguš's [early work on GANs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.03965); [WhAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02206); and recent work on interpretability of deep audio, bioacoustics, and soundscape models. We'll use this insight alongside the skills built in Arc II to begin studying the dynamics and combinatorial properties of sperm whale, orca, and corvid communications, bringing us to the frontiers of statistical modeling in animal linguistics.
